## Arrival in Ireland, 1348

It came in through the ports on the east coast in the summer of 1348, Howth and Dalkey usually named first, then Drogheda. Dublin was hit hard between August and Christmas. The famous figure is 14,000 dead in Dublin in that window, which comes from a single chronicler and is almost certainly too high for a town that size, but it shows the scale people felt.

## Friar John Clyn

The source that makes the whole topic for me. John Clyn, a Franciscan in Kilkenny, kept annals and wrote through the plague as it reached his own friary. His last entry, 1349, is the one I read aloud every year:

> "And I, lest the writing should perish with the writer, ... leave parchment for continuing the work, in case anyone should still be alive in the future."

Then a different hand adds a single line: "Here it seems the author died." The room goes quiet every time. I use the translation in Bernadette Williams' edition (Four Courts, 2007), p. 250.

## What the disease was

*Yersinia pestis*, carried by fleas on black rats, though the rat-only story is now disputed (human fleas and lice probably mattered too). Three forms: bubonic, pneumonic, septicaemic. The DNA confirmation came from the East Smithfield plague pit in London: Bos et al., *Nature*, October 2011. Before that, some historians genuinely argued it was anthrax or a haemorrhagic fever.

The route west is usually traced from the siege of Caffa in the Crimea, 1346, along the trade routes I cover in [[Silk Road trade]], then by ship to Messina in October 1347.

## How many died

- Ole Benedictow: around 60% across Europe. High end.
- More common textbook figure: a third to a half.
- Ireland: towns and the colonists in them seem to have suffered worse than the dispersed Gaelic Irish population in the countryside. Clyn himself says as much.
- Bergen lost a huge share of its people in 1349; the plague arrived on an English ship, see [[Hanseatic League]].

## Aftermath

Labour became scarce and wages rose. England tried to freeze them with the Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and the Statute of Labourers (1351). In Ireland the colony shrank, and by the Statutes of Kilkenny in 1366 the authorities were legislating against colonists adopting Irish language and dress. Not caused by the plague alone, but you can't understand 1366 without 1348.

## Teaching it

Fifth years, source pack BD-5Y-2024: six sources, including Clyn, a Florentine account from Boccaccio's preface to the *Decameron*, and a 14th-century image of flagellants from Tournai.

Things I have learnt to do:

1. Don't let it turn into a gore lesson. Fourteen-year-olds love buboes; they need to get to the wages and the laws.
2. Students will compare with Covid in 2020. Let them, briefly, then ask what's different (germ theory, for one).
3. The "ring a ring o' roses" rhyme has nothing to do with the plague. It's first recorded in the 1880s. I still have to say this every year.

## Reading

- Maria Kelly, *A History of the Black Death in Ireland* (Tempus, 2001), p. 58 for the Dublin figures and why to doubt them.
- Philip Ziegler, *The Black Death* (1969). Old but readable.
- Ole Benedictow, *The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History* (2004). Heavy going, and his death rates are the highest anyone argues for.
